lesson.title: More Than Mendeleev's Cards: Why the Periodic Table Is Organized by Atomic Number
lesson.summary: The periodic table arranges elements so that those with similar properties line up in the same column, an organizing principle first based on atomic mass but later corrected to atomic number once the structure of the atom was understood.
lesson.body:
Elements, the pure substances defined by having a fixed number of protons, their atomic number, had been discovered one at a time for over a century before anyone found a way to organize them systematically. In 1869, the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev built a table by arranging the known elements in order of increasing atomic mass and noticed something striking: their chemical properties repeated in a regular, periodic pattern. Elements that behaved similarly kept landing in the same column if he wrapped his rows at the right points. Mendeleev trusted the pattern so completely that he left gaps for elements nobody had discovered yet, and predicted their properties in advance. When germanium was isolated in 1886, its properties matched Mendeleev's prediction for a missing element he had called eka-silicon almost exactly, a striking early validation of the whole approach.

Mendeleev's mass-based ordering was not perfect, though. Tellurium has an atomic mass of about 127.6 atomic mass units, while iodine's atomic mass is about 126.9, slightly lower. Strict ordering by mass would place tellurium after iodine. But tellurium's chemical behavior clearly matches the column containing sulfur and selenium, while iodine's behavior clearly matches the column containing chlorine and bromine. To keep the properties lined up correctly, tellurium had to be placed before iodine, in defiance of their atomic masses. Mendeleev and others accepted this and similar swaps as necessary exceptions, trusting that some deeper property, not yet understood, must be the true organizing principle.

That deeper property was identified in 1913 by the young English physicist Henry Moseley, who studied the characteristic X-rays given off by different elements when bombarded with electrons. Moseley found a precise, unbroken mathematical relationship between the frequency of an element's X-ray emission and a whole number that increased by exactly one from element to element, a number he correctly identified as the atomic number, the count of protons in the nucleus. Ordering elements by atomic number instead of atomic mass resolved the tellurium-iodine anomaly instantly: tellurium's atomic number is 52 and iodine's is 53, so atomic number correctly places tellurium first, matching its chemical behavior. Moseley's discovery, cut short when he was killed in action in 1915 at age 27, gave chemistry its modern periodic law: the properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic number, not their atomic mass.

Today's periodic table is built on exactly that principle. Elements are arranged left to right in order of strictly increasing atomic number, wrapping into a new row whenever a new principal energy level begins filling with electrons. Elements in the same vertical column, called a group, generally share similar valence electron arrangements and therefore similar chemical behavior, which is why the table's structure is not an arbitrary filing system but a direct map of underlying atomic structure, a relationship explored in full in the next chapter on periods and groups.

The real power of this organization is predictive, not just descriptive. Because position on the table is tied directly to atomic structure, a chemist can look at an element's location and make solid predictions about its reactivity, its typical ionic charge, or its physical properties, even before running a single experiment, exactly the trick Mendeleev pulled off decades before germanium was ever isolated in a laboratory.
